texts.0: SP, due to a late and then oversized bank correction after localizer capture, did not maintain the final approach course within the published tolerance. CDI displacement exceeded 2 dots inside the FAF and the deviation continued to diverge rather than reduce. IP intervention was required to re-establish the aircraft on the localizer.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the CDI with successive bank reversals instead of setting a computed drift-corrected heading, allowed localizer displacement to sit at the 2 dot limit through a long segment of final. The needle was brought back toward centerline only after verbal prompting from the IP. The aircraft was re-aligned late and the correction was still in progress approaching DH.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction angle applied later than the localizer trend required, allowed CDI displacement to open to between 1 and 2 dots after the FAF. SP recognized the trend unprompted and returned the needle toward centerline with a measured heading change well before DH. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP tracked the localizer within 1 dot of CDI displacement throughout the final approach segment. Corrections were small, prompt and flown against a stable heading reference rather than by needle chasing. The aircraft remained on the final approach course to DH.
texts.4: SP held the localizer essentially centered from capture to DH, with CDI displacement negligible at every point of the approach. The drift correction was established on the first heading change and refined only in single-degree increments. There was no perceptible needle movement over the last mile.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the required localizer tolerance but worked consistently on one side of centerline and held it there with repeated small heading reversals. No deviation exceeded standards, yet the pattern shows the wind correction angle being found by trial rather than computed and set. SP is expected to establish a deliberate drift correction so that localizer tracking becomes stable instead of continuously re-corrected.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the localizer with the IP setting a drift-corrected heading and talking through recognizing the trend before it develops. This is SP's first exposure to localizer tracking on an ILS final, and setting a computed drift-corrected heading rather than chasing the CDI has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin setting a drift-corrected heading independently, with the IP available to confirm the correction.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the localizer to the standard expected at this stage, letting CDI displacement sit at the 2 dot limit through a long segment of final before it was brought back toward centerline. The correction followed verbal prompting from the IP rather than SP's own drift-corrected heading. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set a computed drift-corrected heading rather than chasing the CDI with successive bank reversals.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend unprompted, letting CDI displacement open to about 1.5 dots after the FAF before a measured heading change returned the needle toward centerline well before DH. The wind correction angle is still applied later than the localizer trend requires. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the wind correction angle as the localizer trend first appears rather than after it has developed.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the localizer within 1 dot of CDI displacement throughout the final approach segment on most of it, corrections small, prompt and flown against a stable heading reference. One correction was a little larger than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that correction as small as the rest of the segment.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the localizer, letting CDI displacement sit at about the 2 dot limit, at the tolerance limit, before it was brought back toward centerline. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend unprompted, letting CDI displacement open to between 1 and 2 dots after the FAF before a measured heading change returned the needle toward centerline well before DH. Applying the wind correction angle as the trend first appears, rather than after it develops, would keep that displacement smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good localizer discipline.
texts_above.3: SP tracked the localizer within 1 dot of CDI displacement throughout the final approach segment, corrections small, prompt and flown against a stable heading reference rather than by needle chasing, remaining on the final approach course to DH. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good course stability.
texts_above.4: SP held the localizer essentially centered from capture to DH, CDI displacement negligible at every point of the approach, the drift correction established on the first heading change and refined only in single-degree increments. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent localizer precision.

texts.0: SP, due to failing to set an approximate on-glide-path rate of descent at glide slope intercept and then correcting with large pitch changes, did not maintain the glide path within the published tolerance. GSI displacement exceeded 2 dots and the aircraft remained low on the glide path with the deviation still increasing. IP intervention was required to return the aircraft to the glide path.
texts.1: SP, due to correcting glide path deviations with power alone while pitch remained unchanged, allowed GSI displacement to reach and remain at the 2 dot limit. The correction was started only after the IP called the deviation, and the aircraft regained the glide path late in the final segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a rate of descent set slightly high at glide slope intercept, allowed GSI displacement to open to between 1 and 2 dots below the glide path. SP identified the trend on the cross-check without prompting and re-established the correct descent rate with a coordinated pitch and power change. The glide path was regained before DH with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP tracked the glide path within 1 dot of GSI displacement from intercept to DH. Corrections were made with combined pitch and power in small increments, and the rate of descent was reset to the value the approach required rather than repeatedly re-chased. The aircraft remained stabilized on the glide path.
texts.4: SP held the GSI effectively centered throughout the final approach, with deviations negligible at every stage. The descent rate was established at intercept and adjusted only in small, anticipated increments as the groundspeed changed. The approach remained fully stabilized to DH.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the glide path inside the required tolerance but the needle oscillated slowly about centerline for most of the approach. Standards were met, yet the corrections were reactive to the indication rather than anticipatory of the descent rate required. SP is expected to set and trim the correct rate of descent early so that glide path tracking settles instead of cycling.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the glide path with the IP setting an approximate rate of descent at intercept and talking through correcting with coordinated pitch and power. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. texts_at.1: SP tracked the glide path to the standard expected at this stage, letting GSI displacement reach and remain at the 2 dot limit before it was corrected. texts_at.2: SP identified the trend on the cross-check without prompting, letting GSI displacement open to about 1.5 dots below the glide path before a coordinated pitch and power change regained it before DH. SP is expected to set the correct rate of descent at intercept rather than correcting a high rate afterward.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the glide path within 1 dot of GSI displacement from intercept to DH on most of the approach, corrections made with combined pitch and power in small increments and the rate of descent reset to the value the approach required. One correction was slightly larger than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that correction as small as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the glide path, letting GSI displacement reach and remain at about the 2 dot limit, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the trend on the cross-check without prompting, letting GSI displacement open to between 1 and 2 dots below the glide path before a coordinated pitch and power change regained it before DH. Setting the correct rate of descent at intercept, rather than correcting a high rate afterward, would keep that displacement smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound rate-of-descent setting.
texts_above.3: SP tracked the glide path within 1 dot of GSI displacement from intercept to DH, corrections made with combined pitch and power in small increments and the rate of descent reset to the value the approach required rather than repeatedly re-chased, remaining stabilized on the glide path. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed glide-path tracking.

error_modes.label: Computed final approach airspeed after FAF

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management inside the FAF where configuration change, approach checks and radio calls were all left to compete for the same seconds, did not maintain the computed final approach airspeed. Airspeed diverged beyond +15/-10 knots of the computed value and power was applied late and in the wrong sense. IP intervention on the throttle was required to restore the approach airspeed before DH.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the configuration change and the approach checks at the same point on final, allowed airspeed to reach the +15/-10 knot limit relative to the computed final approach airspeed. The power correction was made only after the IP prompted the speed, and the deviation persisted into the final part of the approach.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged after the gear and flap configuration change, allowed airspeed to drift into the band between +10/-5 and +15/-10 knots of the computed value. SP detected the trend on the cross-check without prompting and restored the computed approach airspeed with a single measured power correction. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within +10/-5 knots throughout the segment after the FAF. Power was adjusted in anticipation of the configuration changes rather than in reaction to the airspeed indication, and the speed remained steady through the descent. The approach stayed stabilized on speed to DH.
texts.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with negligible variation from the FAF to DH. Power changes were anticipated for each configuration change and were small enough that the airspeed trace showed no excursion. Speed control did not compete with any other cockpit task.
texts.marginal: SP kept the computed final approach airspeed inside standards but the speed drifted repeatedly toward the slow side after each configuration change before being corrected. Nothing exceeded the required tolerance, yet the corrections were consistently late relative to the configuration change that caused them. SP is expected to sequence the approach tasks so that power is set with the configuration change rather than after the airspeed has already moved.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final segment with the IP sequencing the configuration change and the approach checks and talking through keeping airspeed on the computed value. This is SP's first exposure to sequencing configuration and checks inside the FAF, and keeping them from competing for the same seconds has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin sequencing the approach tasks independently, with the IP available to confirm airspeed.
texts_at.1: SP held the computed final approach airspeed to the standard expected at this stage, letting it reach the plus 15/minus 10 knot limit before power was corrected. The correction followed IP prompting the speed rather than SP's own sequencing of the approach tasks. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to sequence the configuration change and the approach checks so they do not compete for the same seconds on final.
texts_at.2: SP detected the trend on the cross-check without prompting, letting airspeed drift to about 8 knots slow of the computed value before a single measured power correction restored it. Power left unchanged after the gear and flap configuration change is still allowing airspeed to drift before the correction is made. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reset power together with the configuration change rather than leaving it unchanged until airspeed has drifted.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within +10/-5 knots throughout the segment after the FAF on most of it, power adjusted in anticipation of configuration changes rather than in reaction to the indication. One adjustment came a little later than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that adjustment as promptly as the rest of the segment.

texts_above.1: SP held the computed final approach airspeed, letting it reach about the plus 15 and minus 10 knot limit, at the tolerance limit, before power was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP detected the trend on the cross-check without prompting, letting airspeed drift into the band between plus 10/-5 and plus 15/-10 knots of the computed value before a single measured power correction restored it. Resetting power together with the configuration change, rather than leaving it unchanged, would keep that drift smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady power-and-configuration timing.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within +10/-5 knots throughout the segment after the FAF, power adjusted in anticipation of configuration changes rather than in reaction to the airspeed indication so speed remained steady through the descent to DH. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good power anticipation.
texts_above.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with negligible variation from the FAF to DH, power changes anticipated for each configuration change and small enough that the airspeed trace showed no excursion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior speed anticipation.

texts.0: SP, due to an unmonitored rate of descent in the last part of the final segment and no altimeter reference set for the approach, did not respect the published decision height. The aircraft descended below DH without the required visual references, and the subsequent recovery left the aircraft more than 200 ft off the required altitude. IP intervention was required to arrest the descent and start the missed approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that had narrowed onto the course and glide path indications, did not level at the published decision height on the first attempt and reached the 200 ft edge of the tolerance above DH before responding. The level-off was made only after the IP called the altitude, and the aircraft was still settling as the missed approach was started.
texts.2: SP, due to a level-off initiated slightly late for the rate of descent flown, arrived at the decision height with an altitude deviation between 100 and 200 ft above DH. SP identified the deviation unprompted and re-established the required altitude before continuing with the approach decision. Descent below DH did not occur and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew the approach to the published decision height and levelled within 100 ft above DH with no descent below it. The altimeter was correctly set and was included in the cross-check at the correct points of the approach. The DH decision was made at the published altitude.
texts.4: SP arrived at the published decision height with negligible altitude deviation and no descent below DH at any point. The level-off was anticipated from the rate of descent and required no correction after it was made. Altitude awareness at the decision point was precise throughout.
texts.marginal: SP respected the decision height and stayed within standards, but the level-off was made abruptly after the altitude was already approaching the limit of the tolerance. There was no descent below DH, yet the DH was reached without an anticipated lead. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off from the rate of descent so that decision height is captured smoothly rather than caught late.

texts_at.0: SP flew the approach to decision height with the IP calling the rate of descent and talking through anticipating the level-off from it. This is SP's first exposure to leveling precisely at a decision height, and anticipating the level-off from the rate of descent has not yet been built. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin anticipating the level-off independently from the rate of descent, with the IP available to confirm the timing.
texts_at.1: SP controlled altitude at decision height to the standard expected at this stage, reaching the 200 ft edge of the tolerance above DH before responding. The response followed the IP calling the altitude rather than SP's own scan of the course and glide path together with altitude. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep altitude in the scan alongside the course and glide path indications rather than letting the scan narrow onto them alone.
texts_at.2: SP identified the deviation unprompted, arriving at the decision height with an altitude deviation of about 150 ft above DH before the required altitude was re-established. The level-off is still initiated slightly late for the rate of descent flown before the deviation is caught. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to initiate the level-off earlier for the rate of descent flown rather than correcting it after arriving at DH.
texts_at.3: SP flew the approach to the published decision height and levelled within 100 ft above DH with no descent below it on most approaches, the altimeter included in the cross-check at the correct points. One approach needed a slightly later level-off, without descending below DH. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to level off on that approach as promptly as on the rest.

texts_above.1: SP controlled altitude at decision height, reaching about 200 ft above DH, at the tolerance limit, before responding. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the deviation unprompted, arriving at the decision height with an altitude deviation between 100 and 200 ft above DH before the required altitude was re-established. Initiating the level-off earlier for the rate of descent flown, rather than correcting it at DH, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent level-off timing.
texts_above.3: SP flew the approach to the published decision height and levelled within 100 ft above DH with no descent below it, the altimeter correctly set and included in the cross-check at the correct points with the DH decision made at the published altitude. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined decision-height control.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at the published decision height with negligible altitude deviation and no descent below DH at any point, the level-off anticipated from the rate of descent and requiring no correction after it was made. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless decision-height precision.

error_modes.label: Compliance with ATC instructions during the approach

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller and a readback that was never verified against what had been issued, did not comply with the ATC instructions for the approach. The assigned heading and altitude for the intercept were not flown as cleared and the deviation was not detected by SP, with CDI displacement passing 2 dots before it was noticed. IP intervention was required to query ATC and re-establish the cleared profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete readback and an assumption about what the controller had assigned, flew a clearance different from the one issued for the localizer intercept. The error was corrected only after the IP restated the instruction, with CDI displacement reaching 2 dots, at the tolerance limit, and compliance was achieved late relative to the intercept point.
texts.2: SP, due to a readback made while the approach setup was still in progress, initially misapplied part of the ATC instruction for the approach. SP recognized the discrepancy on the next transmission, requested confirmation and complied without prompting and without further consequence to the approach, with CDI displacement staying near 1.5 dots. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP complied with all ATC instructions issued during the approach. Readbacks were complete and in standard phraseology, and each clearance was applied to the aircraft promptly and correctly. No clarification was needed at any point.
texts.4: SP complied with every ATC instruction immediately and accurately, with standard phraseology and readbacks that left no ambiguity. Instructions were anticipated from the approach sequence and applied without any interruption of aircraft control. Radio work never competed with flying the approach.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all ATC instructions but readbacks were rushed and occasionally abbreviated, and one instruction had to be repeated by the controller. Nothing was flown incorrectly, yet the phraseology used leaves room for the intention to be misread on a busy frequency. SP is expected to use full standard readbacks so that compliance is verifiable rather than assumed.

texts_at.0: SP worked ATC instructions on the approach with the IP verifying the readback against what was issued and talking through standard phraseology. This is SP's first exposure to verifying a readback against an issued clearance under approach workload, and doing so consistently has not yet become routine. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin verifying the readback independently against what was issued, with the IP available to confirm the clearance.
texts_at.1: SP complied with ATC instructions for the approach to the standard expected at this stage, letting CDI displacement reach 2 dots, at the tolerance limit, before compliance was achieved. Compliance followed the IP restating the instruction rather than SP's own verified readback. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to verify the readback against what was actually issued rather than assuming what the controller assigned.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the discrepancy on the next transmission without prompting, letting CDI displacement stay near 1.5 dots before requesting confirmation and complying. The readback is still made while the approach setup is still in progress rather than after it settles. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the approach setup before transmitting the readback so it is not made mid-task.
texts_at.3: SP complied with all ATC instructions issued during the approach on most of it, readbacks complete and in standard phraseology, each clearance applied to the aircraft promptly and correctly with localizer displacement staying within 1 dot. One readback needed a brief follow-up, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that readback as clean as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.1: SP complied with ATC instructions for the approach, letting CDI displacement reach about 2 dots, at the tolerance limit, before compliance was achieved. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the discrepancy on the next transmission without prompting, letting CDI displacement stay near 1.5 dots before requesting confirmation and complying. Completing the approach setup before transmitting the readback, rather than mid-task, would remove that discrepancy. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid readback discipline.
texts_above.3: SP complied with all ATC instructions issued during the approach, readbacks complete and in standard phraseology, each clearance applied to the aircraft promptly and correctly with no clarification needed at any point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate compliance.
texts_above.4: SP complied with every ATC instruction immediately and accurately, standard phraseology and readbacks leaving no ambiguity, instructions anticipated from the approach sequence and applied without any interruption of aircraft control. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary radio anticipation.

texts.0: SP, due to an approach plate that was not reviewed against the actual routing before commencing the procedure, violated a published altitude restriction on the intermediate segment. The aircraft was flown below the segment minimum altitude specified in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manual, off by more than 100 ft, and the routing was not corrected by SP. IP intervention was required to restore the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the approach plate segment by segment while already established rather than during the approach briefing, arrived at a step-down fix without the published restriction applied. The restriction was met only after the IP identified it, and the aircraft crossed the fix about 200 ft above the segment minimum, at the limit of the allowable deviation, when compliance was restored.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent started slightly early relative to the published fix, began deviating from the segment altitude profile before the restriction had been cleared. SP checked the plate unprompted, arrested the descent within the allowable band, crossing the fix about 150 ft above the segment minimum, and re-established the published profile before the next fix. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew the published routing and observed all altitude restrictions from MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manual. Each segment minimum was identified before it applied and the descent was initiated only at the published point. The approach profile matched the plate throughout.
texts.4: SP flew the published routing and every altitude restriction precisely, with each segment transition identified before it was reached. Descents were initiated exactly at the published points and the profile required no adjustment at any fix. Plate discipline was complete from the initial segment to DH.
texts.marginal: SP met all published routing and altitude restrictions but confirmed each one only as the fix was reached rather than during the approach briefing. No restriction was violated, yet the margin available to correct an error at any single fix was small. SP is expected to extract the segment altitudes and routing during the briefing so that compliance is planned rather than verified at the last moment.

texts_at.0: SP flew the routing with the IP calling each segment restriction and talking through extracting the segment altitudes during the approach briefing. This is SP's first exposure to extracting published segment restrictions during a briefing, and completing that review before the approach has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin extracting the segment restrictions independently during the briefing, with the IP available to confirm each one.
texts_at.1: SP honored the published altitude restriction to the standard expected at this stage, crossing the step-down fix about 200 ft above the segment minimum, at the limit of the allowable deviation, before compliance was restored. Compliance followed the IP identifying the restriction rather than SP's own approach briefing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the approach plate against the routing during the briefing rather than segment by segment once established.
texts_at.2: SP checked the plate unprompted and arrested the descent within the allowable band, crossing the fix about 150 ft above the segment minimum before the published profile was re-established. The descent is still started slightly early relative to the published fix before the plate check catches it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the descent to the published fix rather than starting it slightly early and correcting afterward.
texts_at.3: SP flew the published routing and observed all altitude restrictions from MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manual on most of the approach, each segment minimum identified before it applied and each crossing altitude met within 100 feet above the published value. One restriction was identified a little later than the rest, without being violated. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to identify that restriction as early as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.1: SP honored the published altitude restriction, crossing the step-down fix about 200 ft above the segment minimum, at the tolerance limit, before compliance was restored. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP checked the plate unprompted and arrested the descent within the allowable band, crossing the fix about 150 ft above the segment minimum before the published profile was re-established. Timing the descent to the published fix, rather than starting it slightly early, would keep that margin steadier. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured profile timing.
texts_above.3: SP flew the published routing and observed all altitude restrictions from MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manual, each segment minimum identified before it applied and the descent initiated only at the published point, the approach profile matching the plate throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise restriction observance.
texts_above.4: SP flew the published routing and every altitude restriction precisely, each segment transition identified before it was reached, descents initiated exactly at the published points with the profile requiring no adjustment at any fix. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate plate discipline.

error_modes.label: ILS setup and standardized procedure sequence

texts.0: SP, due to an approach setup completed out of sequence in which the ILS frequency was not identified and the navigation source was not confirmed, did not execute the procedure according to AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual. The approach was continued with the wrong navigation source displayed and the required approach checks were omitted, with CDI displacement passing 2 dots on the intercept. IP intervention was required to correct the configuration and re-sequence the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the approach setup until after the intercept had begun, executed the standardized sequence with items out of order and the landing configuration established late. The omitted items were completed only after the IP prompted them, and the approach was flown from the FAF with CDI displacement at 2 dots, the tolerance limit, without the sequence having been fully caught up.
texts.2: SP, due to a checklist item deferred while the intercept was being flown, initially omitted one step of the standardized approach sequence. SP detected the omission unprompted at the FAF, completed the item and continued the procedure correctly with no effect on the approach profile, CDI displacement staying within about 1.5 dots. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP executed the ILS approach according to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual. The navigation source was set and identified, the approach checks were completed in sequence and the aircraft was configured at the published points. The procedure was flown without mistakes and without IP intervention.
texts.4: SP executed the standardized ILS procedure flawlessly, with the setup, identification, checks and configuration all completed ahead of the points at which they were required. The sequence was flown with no hesitation and left full capacity available for aircraft control. No item required repetition or correction.
texts.marginal: SP completed the standardized ILS sequence correctly but each item was actioned at the latest acceptable point rather than ahead of it. Nothing was omitted, yet any additional task inside the FAF would have displaced part of the sequence. SP is expected to complete the approach setup and checks earlier so that the procedure absorbs interruptions without slipping.

texts_at.0: SP set up the approach with the IP completing the identification and the approach checks and talking through finishing the setup before the intercept. This is SP's first exposure to a full ILS setup sequence, and completing it before the intercept begins has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin completing the approach setup independently before the intercept, with the IP available to confirm each item.
texts_at.1: SP executed the ILS setup sequence to the standard expected at this stage, flying from the FAF with CDI displacement at 2 dots, the tolerance limit, before the sequence was caught up. Catching up followed the IP prompting the omitted items rather than SP's own approach setup timing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the approach setup before the intercept begins rather than leaving it until after.
texts_at.2: SP detected the omission unprompted at the FAF, letting CDI displacement stay within about 1.5 dots before completing the item with no effect on the approach profile. One checklist item is still deferred while the intercept is being flown before it is caught. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete every checklist item before the intercept is flown rather than deferring one to be caught at the FAF.
texts_at.3: SP executed the ILS approach according to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual on most of it, the navigation source set and identified, the approach checks completed in sequence and localizer displacement inside 1 dot at the FAF. One check was completed a little later than the rest, without a mistake resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete that check as promptly as the rest of the sequence.

texts_above.1: SP executed the ILS setup sequence, flying from the FAF with CDI displacement at about 2 dots, at the tolerance limit, before the sequence was caught up. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.

error_modes.label: Size of heading corrections beyond the 5 degree limit on final

texts.0: SP, due to overcontrolling in heading with corrections far larger than the 5 degree limit taught for course corrections, drove the localizer through centerline on every attempt to recapture it. CDI displacement exceeded 2 dots in both directions and each oversized heading change produced a larger excursion than the one it was meant to remove. IP intervention was required to stop the divergent heading oscillation and stabilize the final approach course.
texts.1: SP, due to heading changes well outside the area beneath the heading bug rather than the 5 degree corrections called for, converted small course errors into repeated overshoots. Localizer displacement reached the 2 dot limit after each recapture and the oscillation was damped only after the IP prompted SP to halve the heading corrections. The aircraft was steady on course only in the last part of the approach.
texts.2: SP, due to a first correction of roughly 10 degrees instead of the 5 degree limit, overshot centerline and allowed CDI displacement to open to between 1 and 2 dots on the opposite side. SP recognized the overcontrol unprompted, reduced the following corrections to within the width of the heading bug and settled the needle well before DH. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP limited heading changes to about 5 degrees, keeping each correction inside the area beneath the heading bug. Localizer displacement stayed within 1 dot and no correction produced an overshoot through centerline. Course control remained stable to DH.
texts.4: SP corrected course exclusively with heading changes of a few degrees taken from beneath the heading bug, so that every correction removed the deviation without generating a new one. Localizer displacement remained negligible throughout the final approach segment. There was no visible overshoot at any point.
texts.marginal: SP held the localizer within tolerance but corrections were consistently sized at the upper end of what the deviation required, occasionally reaching the edge of the heading bug band. Each correction still produced a small overshoot that had to be taken out again. SP is expected to limit heading changes to 5 degrees so that a single correction settles the course instead of starting the next one.

error_modes.label: Drift correction not computed and heading bug not set for final

texts.0: SP, due to not determining the wind from the GPS and not calculating the estimated drift with the 60 to 1 rule, flew the final approach course without any wind corrected heading reference and with no heading bug set. Localizer displacement built past 2 dots downwind and continued to increase because the correction was being searched for rather than applied. IP intervention was required to establish a drift corrected heading on the final approach course.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the heading bug on the last radar vector heading instead of marking the wind corrected heading for final, had no additional visual cue of heading deviations. Localizer displacement drifted out to the 2 dot limit before the trend was recognized, and the drift correction was set only after the IP called the wind. The needle was recentered late on the approach.
texts.2: SP, due to setting the heading bug on the published final approach course without applying the calculated drift, allowed CDI displacement to open to between 1 and 2 dots on the downwind side. SP compared aircraft track on the GPS with aircraft heading, unprompted, moved the bug to the wind corrected heading and reduced the deviation well before DH. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP calculated drift from the known winds before the FAF and marked the wind corrected heading with the heading bug. Localizer displacement remained within 1 dot and heading deviations were visible against the bug as soon as they appeared. Course was maintained to DH.
texts.4: SP computed drift with the 60 to 1 rule, cross checked it against GPS track versus heading and set the heading bug to the wind corrected heading before glide path intercept. The localizer stayed essentially centered and the bugged heading required only single degree refinement. Every deviation was identified against the bug before the CDI moved.
texts.marginal: SP set a wind corrected heading on the bug and remained within tolerance, but the value was arrived at by successive adjustment rather than from a calculated drift, and the bug lagged the heading actually being flown. Localizer displacement stayed inside limits while the reference remained approximate. SP is expected to calculate drift before the FAF and keep the heading bug on the flown wind corrected heading so it works as a deviation cue.

IP intervention was required to stop the vertical oscillation and re-establish the aircraft on the glide path.

texts.2: SP, due to an initial pitch correction of roughly 4 degrees rather than the 2 degree limit, overshot the glide path and allowed GSI displacement to open to between 1 and 2 dots on the opposite side. texts.3: SP corrected glide path deviations with pitch changes limited to 2 degrees, equivalent to about 400 feet per minute on the VSI. GSI displacement stayed within 1 dot and the rate of descent remained close to the 600 feet per minute of the precision final. The glide path was tracked without oscillation to DH.
texts.4: SP flew the glide path with pitch corrections well inside the 2 degree limit, taken as soon as a trend appeared on the GSI rather than after a displacement developed. Displacement remained negligible and the vertical speed stayed within a few tens of feet per minute of 600. No correction was large enough to be visible as a rate change.
texts.marginal: SP kept the GSI within tolerance but corrections repeatedly approached the 2 degree limit for deviations that needed far less, producing small rate excursions either side of 600 feet per minute. No displacement exceeded standards, yet the glide path was being held by a sequence of corrections rather than by a stable descent. SP is expected to scale pitch corrections to the size of the deviation so the rate of descent settles instead of cycling.

IP intervention was required to set an appropriate power and restore the approach profile.

texts.2: SP, due to a single oversized power reduction taken for an airspeed that was only slightly high, allowed airspeed to fall to between 5 and 10 knots below the computed final approach airspeed. SP recognized the overcorrection without prompting, restored torque toward the 21 percent required on the precision final and regained the target airspeed before DH. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP controlled airspeed with small torque adjustments about the setting required for the precision final, reserving larger power changes for excessively high or low airspeed. Airspeed stayed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow of the computed final approach airspeed. Glide path tracking was not disturbed by the power handling.
texts.4: SP held the power essentially at the setting required for the precision final and made only marginal torque adjustments as the descent developed. Airspeed varied by no more than a few knots about the computed final approach airspeed and the aircraft stayed in trim. No power change was large enough to require a pitch correction.

Airspeed remained within limits while requiring continuous throttle activity to keep it there. SP is expected to use small torque adjustments and reserve large power corrections for airspeed that is genuinely excessive.

error_modes.label: Late configuration and unstabilized airspeed and trim at glide path intercept

texts.0: SP, due to configuring far later than the 2 to 3 NM prior to the FAF that allows airspeed and trim to stabilize, was still lowering gear and flaps and running the Before-Landing Checklist as the glide path was intercepted. The out of trim aircraft with changing drag left airspeed beyond 15 knots fast and then more than 10 knots slow of the computed final approach airspeed, with GSI displacement passing 2 dots. IP intervention was required to configure the aircraft and re-establish the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to delaying gear and flaps until the FAF instead of configuring 2 to 3 NM before it, began the descent with the aircraft still accelerating or decelerating and out of trim. Airspeed sat at the limit of 15 knots fast and 10 knots slow of the computed final approach airspeed and the glide path opened to 2 dots while the checklist was completed. Both were brought back only after IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to configuring closer to the FAF than the 2 to 3 NM required for stabilization, entered the descent with trim not yet reset for the approach speed. Airspeed opened to between 5 and 10 knots off the computed final approach airspeed and the GSI moved between 1 and 2 dots during the retrim. SP completed the Before-Landing Checklist and settled speed and trim without prompting before DH.

error_modes.label: Descent gradient not calculated for altitude restrictions inside the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to not calculating the descent gradient required by the published altitude restrictions between the FAF and the runway, flew a rate of descent unrelated to the crossing altitudes on the approach plate. The profile was recovered by successive large changes and the aircraft arrived at decision height more than 200 feet above it with the runway environment not usable. IP intervention was required to correct the descent profile.
texts.1: SP, due to not computing the gradient for the step-down altitudes inside the FAF, held a rate of descent that had to be revised at each fix. The aircraft reached decision height 200 feet high, at the limit of tolerance, and the profile was adjusted only after the IP called the next crossing altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to calculating the descent gradient only after passing the FAF instead of during the approach preparation, entered the segment with a rate of descent that did not match the next altitude restriction. The aircraft was between 100 and 200 feet above the profile before SP recognized the discrepancy, computed the required gradient and corrected the descent unprompted well before decision height.
texts.3: SP calculated the descent gradients for the altitude restrictions inside the FAF and set a rate of descent that satisfied each crossing altitude. The aircraft remained within 100 feet of the required profile and reached decision height within tolerance and never below a published minimum.
texts.4: SP derived the required descent gradient for every restriction inside the FAF before the approach and flew the profile so that each crossing altitude was met without any rate change. The aircraft arrived at decision height with a negligible altitude deviation and with the profile continuous throughout the final segment. No fix required a corrective descent.
texts.marginal: SP met the altitude restrictions inside the FAF and stayed within tolerance, but the descent rate was set from the general profile rather than from a computed gradient and needed a small revision at each fix. No crossing altitude was missed and decision height was reached within limits. SP is expected to calculate the descent gradients during the approach preparation so the profile is flown rather than repeatedly rebuilt.

texts_at.2: SP recognized the discrepancy, computed the required gradient and corrected the descent unprompted well before decision height, the aircraft about 150 feet above the profile before the correction. The gradient is still calculated only after passing the FAF instead of during the approach preparation before the discrepancy appears. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to calculate the gradient during the approach preparation rather than after passing the FAF.
texts_at.3: SP calculated the descent gradients for the altitude restrictions inside the FAF and set a rate of descent that satisfied each crossing altitude on most of the approach, the aircraft remaining within 100 feet of the required profile and reaching decision height within tolerance. error_modes.label: Configuration and approach speed not adjusted for crosswind or gusty conditions

texts.0: SP, due to configuring with the standard flap setting and holding the nominal approach speed in gusty conditions, did not increase airspeed as required for the reported gust factor. Airspeed excursions in the gusts exceeded 15 knots fast and 10 knots slow of the computed final approach airspeed, with pitch and glide path disturbed at each one. IP intervention was required to adjust the configuration and stabilize the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to not increasing airspeed for the gusty wind and correcting the resulting slow indications with pitch, allowed airspeed to reach the limit of 15 knots fast and 10 knots slow of the computed final approach airspeed on successive gusts. The margin was restored only after the IP directed an appropriate speed for the conditions. Glide path tracking was ragged during the same period.
texts.2: SP, due to selecting the approach speed without accounting for the gust factor, saw airspeed swing between 5 and 10 knots either side of the computed final approach airspeed in the turbulence. SP recognized that the conditions required a higher speed, adjusted it unprompted and held the remainder of the approach steady. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP configured with the appropriate flap setting for the conditions and increased airspeed as required for the crosswind and gusts. Airspeed stayed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow of the computed final approach airspeed despite the turbulence, and localizer and glide path remained within 1 dot.
texts.4: SP assessed the crosswind and gust factor before configuring, selected the appropriate flap setting and set an approach speed that absorbed the gusts. Airspeed variation stayed within a few knots of the selected value and course and glide path deviations remained negligible. The added speed was carried without disturbing the descent profile.
texts.marginal: SP added speed for the gusty conditions but did so only after the first significant fluctuation, and the value chosen barely covered the gust factor being experienced. Airspeed stayed within tolerance while the margin above the low end was small on each gust. SP is expected to set the configuration and approach speed for the reported conditions before the FAF rather than in response to the first excursion.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final in gusty conditions with the IP calling the gust factor and talking through increasing approach airspeed for it before the FAF. SP is expected to add the gust correction before the FAF rather than after the first significant fluctuation.
